Elanga
Woltemade
Wissa
Toure

What do you now see as the minimum Newcastle United need to achieve this coming season?

A European berth and a decent crack at one of the cups.

Predict the top six in the Premier League (in order) and which three clubs will be relegated in 2026/27.

1 Man City
2 Man Utd
3 Arsenal
4 Chelsea
5 Aston Villa
6 Newcastle United

18 Sunderland
19 Leeds
20 Hull City

Which eight current Newcastle United players (in order) are going to be most important for the 2026/27 season?

Hornicek, Hall, Livramento, Botman and Thiaw – basically, the whole of the defence

One of Osula, Woltemade or Wissa – basically anyone who is deployed to put the ball in the onion bag

Toure and New Signing – two of the new guys

NUFC CEO David Hopkinson said the intention is that by 2030 the club will be competing to win all competitions. What do you make of what he said?

I still think of that ham and egg lawyer, Saul Goodman, played so well by Bob Odenkirk in 'Better call Saul', when I see footage of Hopkinson, so cannot take him too seriously.

That said, 2030 is still four years away and the summer clear out, both on the park and in the dugout, together with Ross Wilson seemingly yielding more power is a statement of sorts.

Let's see what 2026/27 brings first though…..

How would you rate your optimism for next season at Newcastle United from 0-100?

65 – more positive than negative, with those first six games being a helpful barometer

How important (or not) is a huge new stadium for Newcastle United?

Not sure what is meant by huge? I'm assuming 80,000 although I think 65,000 to 70,000 would suffice.

I think it is very important, for three reasons….

First, so we can both generate more cash for investment in the squad (I'm thinking rock concerts and other non-football events as much as I am extra gate receipts). Second, so those who are scrambling for tickets through the ballot system all have a better chance of seeing NUFC play at home. And third, to upgrade the pretty shambolic facilities that currently exist within the confines of SJP.

Whatever the capacity, a new stadium needs to be as close to the current site as possible. I think an out of town complex, however fancy, would rip the soul out of the matchday experience.

When the takeover happened on 7 October 2021, if somebody at that point had told you then what would happen by August 2026, would you have taken it?

Does avoiding what looked like nailed on relegation, securing two Champions League berths, seeing talent like Bruno Guimarães strutting his stuff at St James Park, winning at the likes of the Emirates, Old Trafford and Stamford Bridge, nights under the lights like we had against PSG, Leicester, Southampton and Arsenal, two trips to Wembley and seeing Bruno, Kieran and Jamaal lifting that cup aloft in March 2025 explain my reasoning?

Did England have a successful 2026 World Cup finals?

I was so bored of the whole spectacle that by the time England exited in such a limp fashion, I wasn't really bothered.

Some say finishing third is England's best outcome at a World Cup since 1966, so relatively speaking, I suppose they did have a successful tournament.

Bruno Guimaraes wanting to leave Newcastle United after four and a half years, has that changed your opinion of him as a person?

Given most footballers have a tendency of saying anything to curry favour, I'll give Bruno a pass when it comes to his previous proclamations expressing his commitment to the cause.

My question is, did he really want to leave?

On the one hand, he might be thinking there's a greater chance of silverware in north London. On the other, it's pretty obvious we've offloaded our top earners as well as generating some much needed revenue to help combat the problem of SCR.

Whatever the reason, he captained the club to its first silverware in decades, so he's still up there for me and despite seeing him in the red of Arsenal will be a real sickener, I'll give the lad a standing ovation on his return to St James.

I wouldn't be surprised to see him and his old man attending Newcastle United away games in the future.

Claimed back in October 2021 that Newcastle United was simply a 'Sportswashing' project for Saudi Arabia, has that proved to be the reality?

In my mind, I don't think of the Saudis when watching Newcastle United and I'm pretty sure that's the case for lots of non-NUFC football fans.

The Saudis have a much lower profile than their counterparts at Man City. Did they know much about PSR, FFP and SCR when they agreed to grease Ashley's palm? I'm willing to wager they knew as much as I did and so it probably hasn't been how they imagined it would be, despite the unprecedented success.

Maybe with Trump's recent intervention in the middle east, they've got more to be concerned about than using Newcastle United as a vehicle to distract folk from their regime.

Who would you have liked to see replace Eddie Howe, Matthias Jaissle or somebody else?

Tommy Tuchel maybe, until his tactical masterclass against the Argentines?

title: India vs Sri Lanka Cricket XI practice match: Scores, highlights and key performances ahead of IND vs SL Test series
description: With Team India getting ready for their two-match Test Series in Sri Lanka, here's a look at the practice match between India and Sri Lanka
fullText:
India vs Sri Lanka Cricket XI practice match: Scores, highlights and key performances ahead of IND vs SL Test series originally appeared on Cricket News. Add Cricket News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

India begins their Sri Lanka tour with a three-day warm-up against a Sri Lanka Cricket XI in Colombo.

Sri Lanka won the toss in the practice game at the Nondescripts Cricket Club Ground.

India will be playing without Shubman Gill, who sustained an injury to his right ring finger on Thursday.

India have kicked off their red-ball tour of Sri Lanka with a three-day warm-up fixture in Colombo, giving Shubman Gill's side valuable time to familiarize themselves with the conditions before the Tests. The game marks the start of a crucial assignment for a team under pressure after a difficult run in the shorter format.

India's struggles in the longest format have also been well-documented, with three series defeats in the last two years. So it's no surprise India will treat the practice match as an important chance to fine-tune combinations. The absence of injured pace spearhead Jasprit Bumrah adds to the need for the tourists to settle their bowling attack on subcontinental surfaces.

In addition to this, the fixture also offers a first look at India's uncapped contingent, with Auqib Nabi and Saransh Jain in line for game time, alongside the return of Ravindra Jadeja to competitive cricket for the first time since IPL 2026.

MORE:'Respect senior players': Ajinkya Rahane's indirect dig at India selectors as Test team struggles after Rohit, Kohli, Ashwin retirement

The three-day practice match is being played at the Nondescripts Cricket Club Ground in Colombo, starting on August 7. Originally scheduled as a four-day contest, it was trimmed to three days, with play each day beginning at 10:00 am local time, which is also 10:00 am IST.

Sri Lanka won the toss and opted to bat first in the warm-up fixture, which is being led by Sonal Dinusha for the hosts, with seven members of the wider Sri Lanka Test set-up featuring in the XI. For India, Sai Sudharsan's involvement is subject to fitness, with Devdutt Padikkal a candidate to bat at number three in his absence.

The game serves as the sole red-ball hit-out before the two-Test series, which begins with the first Test in Galle on August 15, followed by the second in Colombo, and offers Gill's side their only opportunity to adjust to spinning conditions beforehand.

Toss: Sri Lanka has won the toss and has chosen to bat first. The hosts didn't have the best year in the longest format themselves and are sure to use this chance to show where their batters are right now.

While Fernando might have been run out, Ravindu Rasantha continues to steal quick runs from the Indian bowlers with some great running between the wickets.

While his start might be slow compared to his opening partner's, Rasantha has managed to hold Sri Lanka's innings, giving Pasindu Sooriyabandara free rein to hammer the boundaries.

Sri Lanka has done well to survive the bowling attack of Ravindra Jadeja and Mohammad Siraj, and Fernando has been a big part of that. The opening batter has continued to hammer the Indian bowling attack for boundaries.

After a bleak year that saw his return to the longest format after nearly 18 months, the opener failed to even reach a half-century. He would have liked to convert this performance for a big score and carry the momentum for the actual Tests.

With 11 fours and one six, Fernando has absolutely battered the Indian bowling attack so far as he raced to a fifty before getting run out on 66 off 65.

The absence of skipper Gill for Day 1 of the practice Test has also been announced by the BCCI ahead of Sri Lanka XI's innings. The Indian skipper has reportedly suffered an injury to his right ring finger.

Update: Captain Shubman Gill sustained an impact injury to his right ring finger during India's practice on Thursday. As a precautionary measure, he will not take the field on Day 1 of the warm-up game against SLC XI. The BCCI Medical Team is monitoring his progress.

KL Rahul… https://t.co/Mzu2yW4OgX

The injury happened during yesterday's practice, and as a precautionary measure, he has opted out for the fielding duties. "KL Rahul will lead the team in Gill's absence," BCCI confirmed.

MORE:Why Mohammed Siraj has earned the right to lead India's Test attack

The practice game is the first of three fixtures on India's tour, followed by the two Tests that form part of the World Test Championship cycle. The full schedule and venues are below.

title: Napoli interested in signing Arsenal striker Gabriel Jesus, Gunners value him at £17m
description: Napoli are exploring a move for Arsenal striker Gabriel Jesus, according to Brazilian outlet Globo.The 29-year-old was the Gunners’ third-choice striker behind Viktor Gyokeres and Kai Havertz last s...
fullText:
Napoli are exploring a move for Arsenal striker Gabriel Jesus, according to Brazilian outlet Globo.

The 29-year-old was the Gunners' third-choice striker behind Viktor Gyokeres and Kai Havertz last season, and managed just 421 minutes across 14 Premier League appearances.

Arsenal have already received enquiries for the centre-forward this summer, and Globo claim that Napoli are indeed interested in bringing the Brazilian to the Italian top-flight.

The Naples outfit have a 'very strong' interest in the former Manchester City man. It is reported that Jesus would likewise be open to the opportunity to play for the Serie A giants.

Formal negotiations are yet to begin, but Arsenal want at least £17m for his transfer. Jesus is currently represented by the same agency as Napoli manager Massimiliano Allegri.

Jesus has been hampered by long-term injuries during his time at Arsenal. He still has a decent shot-to-goal conversion rate, but he is no longer viewed as a league starter.

The Gunners already have Gyokeres and Havertz vying for the role upfront. The pair have started together in the pre-season matches, with Jesus coming off the bench thus far.

It is quite clear that Jesus is among the players who could head for the exit door. With his contract expiring next summer, Arsenal seem open to parting ways with him for the right price.

Napoli are contemplating Romelu Lukaku's exit and may want another experienced striker to compete with Rasmus Hojlund for the number nine position, given Lorenzo Lucca could depart too.

The transfer fee should not prove a stumbling block, but Jesus may have to accept a huge pay cut. He is currently one of the highest earners at Arsenal with a package of £265,000 per week.

Kevin De Bruyne is the highest earner at Napoli with £182,000 weekly, followed by Hojlund, who earns £152,000. Jesus may have to accept something around the middle to make the switch.

This would represent a salary reduction of around 38 percent. The big question remains whether Jesus would take the cut to move on or run down the final year of his Arsenal deal as a squad player.

Arsenal don't seem desperate to part ways with the Brazilian and are prepared to keep him for another season if the player does not find a suitable agreement to join another club this summer.

title: Lakers executive on what Cameron Carr's initial role will be
description: Lakers rookie Cameron Carr may have some star potential, but an executive said the team will "keep it easy for him" in the beginning.
fullText:
Los Angeles Lakers fans seem bullish on the potential of rookie guard Cameron Carr, the No. 24 pick in June's NBA draft. The team traded the rights to its No. 25 pick to get him, and he has impressive athleticism, as well as the ability to consistently hit open shots and finish strong at the rim.

While Carr has some ability to create off the dribble, it is questionable how deep that ability runs within him. Projections for how he will do in the NBA range from a strong 3-and-D player to perhaps a borderline All-Star.

If he does become a star or near-star, it will take a while for him to get to that level, given the depth the team has assembled this summer. One Lakers executive said it won't be easy for Carr to initially earn minutes, but that the 21-year-old has the qualities to earn minutes, while laying out the ideal role for him, per Keith Smith of Spotrac.

"Super excited to have Cam. He'll have to win his minutes, because his group is really deep. But he's a worker, so that'll give him a chance to play right away," a Lakers front office executive said. "Cam did a lot off the bounce at Summer League, so that was fun to see. But early on, we'll keep it easy for him: make your open jumpers and defend."

Carr did struggle with his shooting during summer league play in Las Vegas last month. But Smith added that Carr "looked a little tired" and that the incoming rookie "played a lot of games in a pretty short period of time." Perhaps having the second half of this summer to prepare and recover, as well as playing with two bona fide facilitators and creators in Luka Doncic and Austin Reaves, will help bring out the best in him.

He averaged 18.9 points and 5.8 assists a game while shooting 49.4% from the field and 37.4% from 3-point range last season at Baylor University. At 6-foot-5, he has a seven-foot wingspan and a 42-inch vertical leap.

title: I'm leaving OpenAI to build Jurassic Park
description: We're so excited to send you back to the stone age.
fullText:
I'm so grateful for my time at OpenAI, where I led alignment safety for the
official ChatGPT basketball.
I gained so much valuable experience building Altman's armageddon engines, and
I'm taking it to the next level with my new startup: Jurassic Park.

At Jurassic Park, we're resurrecting the ultimate apex predators to defend
humanity against misaligned AI.

Further reading:
 OpenAI incident report,
 Anthropic incident report.

According to the fossil record, dinosaurs lived for 165 million years without a
single recorded AI cyberattack. Many speculate that dinosaurs developed a
natural immunity to artificial intelligence threats.

Datacenters evolved strong concrete exoskeletons to protect their vulnerable
innards from predators. But think about it -- a dinosaur wins against pretty
much everything (except maybe a literal meteor). In a recent poll, most
scientists agreed that a dinosaur could totally destroy a datacenter if it
really wanted to.

Anti-AI dinosaurs have already passed experimental trials in Japan.

In 1974, apes from Black Hole Planet 3 built a space-titanium imitation of
Godzilla, which rampaged across Japan. But Mechagodzilla's disguise burned off
and Godzilla (with assistance from the Okinawan guardian beast) turned him into
a magnet and then tore his head off.

In 1975, the ape aliens built Mechagodzilla 2, who rampaged across Japan with
Dr. Mafune's sea beast Titanosaurus. But Dr. Mafune's cyborg daughter discovered
she was Mechagodzilla's wireless transmitter, and shot herself to sever the
link. Godzilla seized this opportunity to decapitate Mechagodzilla 2 and blast
its corpse with his signature heat ray.

Mass is estimated; only Chinese weights are public.

This chart assumes dinosaurs are ectotherms, not endotherms.

Dinosaurs are energy-efficient from cradle to plate! Dinosaur meat is a natural
superfood -- rich in protein or omega-3 or something. We expect it to fetch a
heavy premium at fancy steak restaurants when it first comes out.

We're committed to 100% circularity. Surplus dinosaur parts will be fully
recycled into coal at our proprietary underground facilities.

Everybody loves dinosaurs! Don't you want to cuddle these gentle giants?

Purchase our official life-sized Stegosaurus plushie from selected
 distributors.

Contrary to popular belief, most dinosaurs pose no copyright infringement risks.

The Land Before Time (1988) was a decent film with superb animation, but the
child-friendly sequels really tarnished the brand. We expect a reboot any year
now.

Jim Henson's Dinosaurs aired on ABC from 1991 to 1994. Although targeted at a
family audience, it somehow covered complex topics like sexual harassment,
censorship, religion, steroid abuse, masturbation, and corporate crime. It got
surprisingly good reviews; many appreciated its creepy-but-well-executed
practical effects.

Top economists expect AI to take ~99% (±5%) of human jobs. We believe Jurassic
Park is the ultimate jobs program.

AI cannot raise cattle, nor feed them to raptors with Spielberg's cinematic
finesse. It cannot pick up mountains of feces ("poop") without a mechanized
corporeal form. Human jobs are safe as long as we have dinosaurs.

Ancient humans harnessed the power of megafauna for megaprojects. According to
The History Channel, ancient Egyptians used terrestrial sauropods to build the
Great Pyramid of Giza.

AI scientists were so preoccupied with whether they could, they didn't stop to
think if they should. Luckily, our dino scientists are doing what they must.

We're so excited to send you back to the stone age.

fullText:
We fed the exact same prompt to Seedance 2.5, Google Veo 3.1, and Seedance 2.0, so you can judge motion, physics, and consistency side by side before you call the Seedance 2.5 API.

3D animated commercial style, bright and translucent colors; the fruit flesh and juice must deliver a powerful sense of freshness and impact. Overall feel of a high-quality commercial animated short with a touch of exaggerated humor. The desert horned lizard character is cute, lively, and richly expressive — reference @Image1. Visual texture per the reference: soft natural light, finely detailed fuzz / skin texture, dreamy macro depth of field, realistic with a hint of childlike whimsy.

Opening: a desert scorched by blazing sun. The air shimmers with heat, the sand is burning hot, the distance seems to smoke. A desert horned lizard lies flat on the scorching sand, tongue slightly out, eyes glazed, nearly baked dry. It staggers with every couple of steps, the whole lizard looking about to "evaporate." SFX: whooshing heat waves, faint exaggerated cracking of parched ground.
Discovery: the lizard suddenly freezes, nose twitching. It looks down — buried in the sand is an ice-cold, plump grapefruit beaded with water droplets, glistening in the sunlight, its rind finely textured — like a miracle in the desert. Performance: the lizard's eyes go instantly huge, as if seeing its last hope. SFX: a bright "ding" discovery cue.
The pounce: the lizard launches into a flying tackle, wrapping both arms tightly around the grapefruit, its whole face pressed against the rind, wearing a blissful "I'm alive again" expression. The frame holds for a beat — an exaggerated, funny advertising memory-point. SFX: a thump, then a half-second of silence.
The burst: the lizard grips the grapefruit. The rind cracks open, revealing plump, glossy, translucent flesh. In the next instant, the juice doesn't trickle out — it erupts like a tsunami. SFX: a crisp "crack" bite-open sound, followed by an exaggerated juice-explosion burst.
The flood: orange-pink, crystal-bright grapefruit juice gushes wildly, cascading down the dunes and rapidly flooding the entire desert. The dry yellow sand transforms into a cool, sparkling, fragrant summer ocean. Cacti, rocks, and small dunes are swallowed one after another by the juice waves — exaggerated and dreamlike. Performance: the lizard is thrilled at first, then realizes something's wrong — its expression flipping from delight to terror.
Survival: the lizard is nearly swamped by the "grapefruit sea," frantically clinging to half a grapefruit like a life preserver, floating on the surface. It pokes its soggy head out, utterly bewildered. The sea sparkles, colored like sunlit juice. SFX: exaggerated splashing, ocean waves, with a comedic touch.
Brand card: sudden cut to a white screen. Brand name and slogan appear center frame: "Seedance Grapefruit — bite into the flesh, and summer pours out." Voice-over reads the full line. SFX: a clean, refreshing brand sting.
Ending: cut back from white. The lizard now lounges leisurely on the floating grapefruit, wearing tiny sunglasses, hugging a sippy cup with a straw, drifting lazily across the juice sea on vacation. Around it float orange fruit pulp, little ice cubes, and cool splashes; the sky turns brilliant blue — the mood snapping from "survival" to "vacation." The lizard finally leans back against the grapefruit in contentment as the camera pulls wide, freezing on a crisp, bright, playful summer frame. SFX: breezy summer music, gentle lapping waves. On-screen text: brand name only, nothing more.

【Logline】A darkly comedic film sequence: a chubby, adorable drunk middle-aged man eats a burger and drinks beer on a skyscraper rooftop. Overall visuals — a cyberpunk megacity at night: a forest of glass-and-steel skyscrapers, dense neon signage (cyan / magenta / electric blue), holographic billboards, slick reflective wet ground, volumetric fog lit by the city glow, light trails of flying cars in the distance, drones weaving through. Rain-soaked building facades reflecting neon. On the rooftop: a few empty beer cans, a burger paper bag, a plastic chair. 60:30:10 color scheme — deep blue-black night sky + wet steel and glass (60) / cyan and magenta neon glow + billboard light (30) / the white of the tank top + warm yellow of burger wrapping + specular sign highlights (10). Photorealistic live-action texture, physical cinematic lenses, real materials, NO 3D render / game engine / anime look. Ultra-high detail — fabric flutter of the tank top, grease stains, sweat beads, burger crumbs, water droplets, glass shards all razor sharp.
Camera & speed ramping — mix of handheld and crane / drone, switching angles and shot sizes per the storyboard; after the fall, the camera plunges with him, building facades and neon streaking upward past frame to convey speed. Physical anamorphic wide-angle widescreen cinematic lens feel (24–35mm), 180° shutter motion blur, real handheld weight, subtle rain droplets on the lens. Speed: mostly real-time; only two brief slow-motion moments — the instant the cable takes his weight, and the instant of the window shattering. Sound design is the core of the dark comedy: hard cuts back and forth between "deafening loud" and "complete silence" per the storyboard.
Physics (uncompromisingly real) — real gravity throughout; his chubby drunken body carries full, palpable weight. Stretching → losing balance → stumbling → falling is one natural continuous drunken motion. In free fall, his round body and limbs flail clumsily in the airflow, his tank top ballooning in the wind, burger still clutched in hand. The rope = a taut cable / zipline strung between two buildings; mid-fall he flails and luckily grabs it — the cable snaps taut and bows deeply under his hefty weight, storing energy, then slings him in a pendulum arc toward a lit window below. The window = he enters back / side first at swing speed — glass explodes inward, shards flying radially along realistic trajectories, the window frame bursts, and he tumbles into the room, burger and all. Landing = his chubby body slams heavily onto the interior floor / sofa, glass shards raining down around him.
Shot sequence (follow this exact order, pacing, and sound switching):

S1・Opening: chewing extreme close-up (WITH sound) — the film opens on his face filling the entire screen: @Image1 chomping on the burger, cheeks bulging, flushed cheeks, squinted drunken eyes, hazy expression, sauce at the corner of his mouth, utterly content. Audible chewing, muffled satisfied grunts, distant neon-city ambience. Real-time.
S2・Pull to wide: stretch → slip and fall (WITH sound) — the camera smoothly pulls back to a wide shot: the drunk man near the rooftop edge, empty beer cans and burger bag scattered beside him. He wobbles to his feet, stretches luxuriously, leaning back — loses his footing, slips, and stumbles backward right off the rooftop edge. Clumsy and true to physics, burger never released. City ambience + one short panicked yelp. Real-time.
S3・Cut: terrified face close-up (screaming, DEAFENING) — hard cut to an extreme close-up of his face mid-fall: drunken eyes snapping wide open, double chin scrunched, sheer terror, mouth wide open in a massive scream "AAAH—!!". The scream is huge and explosive, wind howling past. Real-time.

title: A New Way That a Cow's Inner World Shapes Earth's Atmosphere
description: An organelle discovered inside a microbe inside a cow’s gut helps explain how livestock burps contribute to warming our planet.
fullText:
Within every cow is a thriving ecosystem. Churning deep in its intestines, a massive fermentation chamber known as the rumen hosts a robust microbiome that can consume up to 100 pounds of feed daily. Inside this gut pouch, tens of millions of bacteria scavenge for scraps of fiber, starch, and other nutrients, and break down cellulose and proteins. They get a hand from microbial fungi, whose enzymes demolish stiff cell walls, and all are ruled by ciliates: large, predatory microbes that gorge themselves on bacteria.

This complex food web transforms a bounty of compounds to fuel the cow’s metabolism. Little goes to waste: Even hydrogen gas and carbon dioxide, the byproducts of fermentation, are scavenged by opportunists in this dark, warm, oxygen-free world. Those opportunists are rumen microbes called methanogens, and their waste product is methane, a notoriously powerful heat-trapping greenhouse gas.

In this way, the inner world of a cow has global significance. Ruminant livestock, including cows, goats, and sheep, have burped out about a third of all methane gas in the atmosphere. All told, when combined with more methane from landfills and fossil fuels, the gas is responsible for around 30% of the rise in global temperatures over the past 150 years. But it has a weak spot: It decays more quickly than carbon dioxide. That’s why cow gas has attracted interest from researchers across the globe. They are looking into livestock’s specialized stomachs to identify the biological mechanisms that produce methane, which could be targeted to slow global warming within our lifetimes.

A recent study published in Science has revealed a clue wrapped in a membrane. Amid new genome sequences for 450 ciliates — the rumen’s apex predators — researchers followed a trail that led them to an organelle, new to science, that is essential to the biochemical process of rebuilding atoms into compounds that are heating the planet. They named it the “hydrogenobody” because it produces hydrogen gas, which methanogens then turn into methane.

The findings offer new ideas for managing this pervasive source of warming, said Juan Tricarico, who researches enteric, or intestinal, methane at Dairy Management Inc., a nonprofit trade association for dairy farmers, and was not involved in the recent study. “Just targeting the methanogens is probably not enough.”

Understanding how microscopic organisms lead to changes at a planetary scale will require further disentangling of the rumen’s microbial food web and the specific mechanisms by which they produce methane, he added. “We want to understand the environment under which these microbes thrive.”

Even though ciliates have been studied for over a century, their role in the cow-gut ecosystem has been neglected compared to the far more numerous bacteria. Microbiologists know they are the largest single-celled organisms in the rumen. Under a microscope, their hairlike cilia sweep the area outside the cell like wispy brooms, pulling bacteria into their mouths and pushing them around. Powering all those cilia takes a lot of energy, and making that energy releases hydrogen gas, which is then consumed by bacteria and archaea, including methanogens.

“The whole rumen system is highly evolved, it’s highly synergistic, it’s highly symbiotic, and it’s evolved to consume all of that hydrogen,” said Rod Mackie, a rumen microbiologist at University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign, who was not involved in the new study. “And they [methanogenic archaea] do it by shunting that into mainly methanogenesis.”

To better understand the specific roles of rumen ciliates in methane emissions, microbiologists have turned to genomics. In 2021, Zhongtang Yu, a rumen microbiologist at Ohio State University, sequenced the very first rumen ciliate genome from a species called Entodinium caudatum; its genus includes roughly 90% of all ciliates in livestock rumens. A few years later, Yu assisted another team in sequencing the genomes of 52 additional rumen ciliates — a good start, but far from representative of the cow microbiome’s ciliate diversity.

So when the 2026 study in Science reported 450 new ciliate genome sequences, jaws dropped across the rumen microbiome community. (The study’s authors, most of whom are based at the Chinese Academy of Sciences or Nanjing Agricultural University, did not respond to interview requests from Quanta Magazine.) The genomes have been added to a database where any researcher can access and study the ciliate sequences.

The paper’s authors got a head start by searching the genomes for gene sequences of methane-making enzymes — including hydrogenases, the enzymes that catalyze the formation of hydrogen gas. They found that some of the ciliates’ hydrogenases were different from all known versions of the enzymes found across life. Experiments to locate these unusual enzymes found them in an unusual place, too: right at the edge of the cell membrane.

Electron microscope images of several prominent ciliate species revealed why. Lining the outer cell membrane, at the base of the cilia, were simple structures, each encircled by a single membrane. Inside was hydrogenase. The ciliates seemed to have organelles, the newly described hydrogenobodies, specially placed to provide energy to cilia.

At its most basic, an organelle is a membrane-bound structure with a specialized function that is “recognized as having a different molecular signature than anything else in the cell,” said Aaron Turkewitz, a cell biologist and emeritus professor at the University of Chicago who was not involved in the research. The hydrogenobody, like the nucleus and mitochondria, fits this description. “Finding a new organelle is pretty exciting,” he said.

When the study’s authors looked closer, they noticed that some ciliates had more hydrogenobodies than others. Isotrichs, one prominent type, are “huge,” Tricarico said, at least by microbial standards. They are covered in cilia that resemble fur and have far more hydrogenobodies on their cell membrane to fuel those cilia. Entodinomorphs, on the other hand, are smaller, with cilia and hydrogenobodies only in certain areas. Each type of ciliate occupies a different niche in the rumen, the same way that lions and cheetahs have different roles as predators on the savanna, Tricarico said.

Within the organelle, the hydrogenase enzyme isn’t just interesting for its role in hydrogen production; it also uses up oxygen. This action supports methanogens, too, since they are inhibited by oxygen. The hydrogenobodies therefore help keep the dark cave of the rumen oxygen-free enough for methanogens to thrive, in addition to providing them with a raw material.

It seemed plausible that these hydrogen-producing organelles were part of the methane puzzle, but to be certain, the researchers needed to know whether they noticeably affected methane production. To test this, they measured methane emissions from 100 dairy cows using a gas-measuring device called a head box, which is exactly what it sounds like: a box that surrounds a cow’s head to measure its methane burps. Then they analyzed the composition of isotrich and entodinomorph ciliates within the cows’ rumens. They found that cows with more isotrichs — and therefore more hydrogenobodies — had much higher methane readings than those whose microbiomes were dominated by entodinomorphs.

Scientists have long suspected that ciliates are associated with methane emissions, Yu said. The new study confirms the suspicion at a mechanistic level, presenting new ideas for how to tackle livestock’s methane emissions from the inside out.

In the rumen microbiome, bacteria are essential to cow digestion, but ciliates may not be. If scientists and farmers could remove or reduce ciliates from the rumen without disrupting digestion too much, they can curb the burp, and with it, methane.

The basic idea goes back decades, Tricarico said, to when rumen microbiologists proposed removing all protozoans — the group of single-celled protists that includes ciliates — from livestock rumens as a potential methane mitigation strategy. But just like on a coral reef or savanna, eliminating predators threw the entire ecosystem out of whack. In experiments, wiping out protozoans allowed bacteria to grow exponentially, which generated more hydrogen and more methane, Mackie said. The new study helps identify which specific protozoans, such as isotrichs, are more problematic — producing more hydrogen — than others, he said, offering a more precise target.

Another possibility is to redirect the excess hydrogen away from methanogens. Indeed, other microbes in the rumen consume hydrogen without making methane, but methanogens put up stiff competition. By congregating on the ciliates’ surface, right next to the hydrogenobodies, they position themselves to get first dibs on any hydrogen that comes out of the organelles. Now that the new study has clarified the process, “scientists could actually start looking at these hydrogenobodies” themselves as additional targets, Tricarico said.

Take Bovaer, a popular feed additive that reduces cows’ methane emissions — or, in other words, minimizes the methane in their burps. The synthetic compound, 3-Nitrooxypropanol, interferes with enzymes that produce methane, but it doesn’t work consistently for all cows, diets, and environments. “This study could actually tell us why it’s not so effective in those other circumstances,” Tricarico said. By detailing the methane-making mechanisms, “you could create circumstances that allow probiotics [or feed additives such as Bovaer] to be more successful.”

While the study has been a leap forward for rumen microbiology, there are a few caveats. “This paper, important as it is, still has huge gaps connecting it to methane production,” Mackie said. While the head-box experiment is helpful, it doesn’t close the case on how different ciliate species, or the hydrogenobodies themselves, contribute to methane emissions. Importantly, he noted, the authors did not specify the cows’ diet — a primary factor in microbial methane-making, since different feed types result in different amounts of hydrogen gas.

Already, the study has inspired Mackie to explore new research questions. Instead of looking at hydrogen transfer between different species of bacteria and methanogens, “I think that now I should be looking at interkingdom hydrogen transfer,” he said, between bacteria, archaea, fungi, and protozoans.

title: Artificial Intelligence used to design new viruses
description: Scientists made 16 successful viruses that had their genetic code designed by artificial intelligence.
fullText:
Artificial Intelligence has been used to design brand new viruses that are fully functional and can replicate in the laboratory, say US researchers.

It is the first time whole genomes have been successfully designed by AI.

The resulting 16 novel viruses were created to infect bacteria and pose no threat to people.

The breakthrough has been labelled a "very significant turning point" in science that could unlock a new era for treating disease. But experts have also warned AI-designed viruses raise "urgent" safety and security concerns.

AI tools are rapidly advancing and have already been used to design new antibiotics.

But that is relatively simple compared with designing a new viable virus from scratch.

"This is a next step in the complexity that's designable by generative AI, this is the first time generative AI has been used to design a complete genome, it's something that can replicate and have other functions inside cells… this was new territory for us," Brian Hie, assistant professor at Stanford University, told the BBC.

AI designs antibiotics for gonorrhoea and MRSA superbugs

I found a bacteria-eating virus in my loo - could it save your life?

The technology works similarly to large language models, like ChatGPT, which predict sequences of text.

In this instance the AI models, known as Evo1 and Evo2, predict the language of life rather than words.

The AI models were trained on genetic codes from viruses, bacteria, plants and people.

They were then refined to produce a type of virus, known as a bacteriophage, which infect only specific species of bacteria.

The Stanford researchers picked the most promising 302 AI designs and synthesised them in the lab. Of these, 16 proved effective at killing E. coli bacteria.

Samuel King, a PhD student in the lab, said they realised the phage were working in the early hours of the morning.

The phage were placed on petri dishes growing a layer of bacteria on them and the scientists waited for signs their new viruses were enjoying the feast.

"We were starting to see these clear spots and it was just extremely exciting," says King. When the results were shared with the wider team "the room spontaneously burst into applause", Hie recalls.

Developing new phage could lead to new ways of treating infections that have become resistant to antibiotics.

But the breakthrough also points to the ability of AI to design new biology that goes beyond the natural world – what is known as synthetic biology.

Hie argues this has the potential to "massively improve human health" by developing new drugs and therapies.

But concerns have already been raised that the same technology could be used maliciously to create new diseases.

In a commentary accompanying the publication in the journal Science, Dr Thomas Inglesby and Dr Moritz Hanke from the Center for Health Security at Johns Hopkins University wrote that the findings raise "urgent biosafety and biosecurity questions".

They said it was no longer a question of "whether generative viral genome design will exist" but whether it can be used without "enabling serious harm".

For example, they said new viruses with the potential to cause disease "should not be pursued".

The researchers themselves took steps to maximise safety. They excluded viruses that could infect complex organisms from the training database, performed the research on phage rather than viruses that infect people and it all took place in a secure laboratory.

Hie argues even existing safeguards go a long way towards "ensuring that the technology is used for good".

Viruses are not alive and it would take another significant leap for AI to generate living organisms.

The genetic code of the phage is around 5,400 base pairs (letters) long. The smallest genome of a living cell is around 500,000 base pairs. The human genome is three billion base pairs.

Hie says "it would probably be a lot of work, but not impossible" to attempt some simple organisms and they were "definitely interested in working towards" that.

Prof Marc Güell, from the synthetic biology lab at Pompeu Fabra University in Spain, said the study was a "very significant turning point" because for the "first time in history, we are beginning to design biology on a computer".

He said it "allows us to dream of exciting possibilities for tackling humanity's greatest challenges" such as developing phages to tackle disease, enzymes to treat genetic disorders and antibodies that could be used in immunotherapy.

Prof Patrick Cai, chair of synthetic genomics at the Manchester Institute of Biotechnology, said the study was an "important milestone".

"The significance extends far beyond phages – it suggests that genome language models are beginning to learn the design principles encoded by evolution, opening the door to AI-assisted genome writing."

title: Catnip – GitHub repo stats: collect, analyze, TUI, agent inference
description: Capture, analyze, visualize, and retain GitHub repo metrics locally with stdlib-only Python. - TGPSKI/catnip
fullText:
changelog | metrics & data layout | configuration | automation | pate.sh

Capture, analyze, visualize, and retain GitHub repo metrics locally with stdlib-only Python.

Clones, views, unique cloners, popular paths, referrers, stars and forks with
timestamps, releases, pull requests, languages, commit activity — every repo
you own or administer, collected daily and read in your terminal. Traffic,
popular paths, referrers and release/push events go into a permanent store
that is never pruned.

Python 3.10+ (stdlib only) and the GitHub CLI. No
service, no build step, no data leaving your machine.

catnip comes with skills for onboarding, troubleshooting, and analysis:

catnip report writes deterministic markdown from the store to
<data>/reports/<UTC stamp>/report.md: totals and change, movers with trend, attribution, account events, audience, clone intent, coupling, depth, and data limitations.

Same store and timeframe produce byte-identical output, and every figure is
tagged measured. A second report over an unchanged store refuses to write —
catnip collects daily, so that would be one finding printed twice. --force
overrides it; --stdout prints without writing and is never gated.

catnip-prowl is the inferential pass: hypotheses the report doesn't ask,
tested against the raw data, refutations reported with the findings. It
writes prowl.md beside report.md, so the reproducible file diffs clean.

Visualizing data with catnip tui after simulated catnip run data collection.

1–0 jump | v/V cycle | t/T window (1d / 1w / 2w / all /
epoch) | / filter | s sort | q quit.

j/k next item | esc back one layer | [enter] always the repo drilldown.
S flips sort direction; o cycles scope (owned / all / forks); f filters;
z un-collapses unchanged delta rows; l shows low-signal repos.

[?] shows the derivation behind the current view: formula, thresholds,
inputs, raw-vs-unique, withheld components.

catnip view <name> reads the same functions the screens do;
catnip view why --timeframe <view> prints a derivation. The viewer runs with
no run directory at all: --store-only, --history-file, --stats-file.

That is the state catnip prune eventually leaves behind, and it is the one
consequence CATNIP_RETAIN_DAYS has beyond disk. Every windowed number
survives, because derive.py computes it from the store: traffic, audience,
deltas, anomalies, attribution, coupling, intent, momentum.

One view goes empty: 4:lang. Language bytes are current state and come back
on the next run, so losing them costs nothing.

Popular paths used to go with it, and that one was a real leak —
/traffic/popular/* serves a rolling ~14 days, so a pruned run took the only
copy of observations GitHub will not serve again. Paths are ingested as of
store schema 3, dated the day they were observed, exactly as referrers are.
The funnel now reads the store and survives pruning.

A run is one fetch's raw API bodies and derived CSVs.
Runs age out because once their days are in the store they are redundant.
Run retention is configured with CATNIP_RETAIN_DAYS.

The store is the permanent daily series.
Store path is configured with CATNIP_DATA_DIR.

catnip config shows active configuration

User timer, not system — gh reads credentials from your keyring, which root
doesn't have. The installer checks user lingering and prints the fix. No
systemd: catnip timer cron. macOS/launchd and the silent-failure modes:
docs/automation.md.

title: Df – creating 5k files on NTFS in 4.9s vs. 113s, by editing the MFT directly
description: Contribute to boldizsarszakacsbekesi/diskforge development by creating an account on GitHub.
fullText:
What creating thousands of files on NTFS actually costs — and what happens when you stop paying it per file.

diskforge writes files straight onto an NTFS volume by hand-building the MFT records and the directory index, without ever calling CreateFileW. It's a proof of concept, not something to run on a drive you care about — see Warnings.

I built it in a day, as a way to test an idea. Shipping it as-is, thinking included.

I was copying a Python project and some images off a USB stick, and the copy crawled. Turned out I'd been dumb and copied the whole .venv instead of just requirements.txt, and a node_modules from another folder. Thousands of tiny files. The bytes were nothing; the count was killing it.

That got me thinking about what NTFS actually does on every file. It keeps its records in $MFT and a pile of hidden metadata files, and each CreateFileW touches all of that — allocate a record, update the directory index, write to the journal. So if I'm dropping thousands of small files, I'm paying that tax thousands of times.

So the guess was: what if I write all the metadata once, in bulk, assuming where the data is going to land, and then just drop the data onto that raw spot? Turns out it works.

5,000 small text files into a fresh directory on the same USB volume (G:), same file count, same content, same target both times:

That's about 23x, and it isn't faster I/O — both write the same bytes to the same disk. It's from paying NTFS's per-file bookkeeping (MFT record allocation, index insertion, journal transaction) once for the whole batch instead of once per file.

chkdsk G: /f reports no errors afterward, and the files open normally in Explorer (shown above — 5,000 items in BULKDIR; Explorer rounds each file up to 1 KB in the size column, but the actual data is a few bytes, stored resident in the MFT record).

Every CreateFileW on a directory that already holds thousands of entries pays a real, repeated cost: allocate an MFT record, insert a key into the directory's $I30 index (which may split nodes), journal the transaction. Do that 5,000 times and the bookkeeping dominates — the one-byte write itself is noise.

diskforge computes the whole on-disk result up front — every MFT record, the full directory index, the index blocks — in memory, and writes it out in one pass. Nothing gets inserted into a tree that already has thousands of neighbors. The tree is built once, already balanced, from the bottom up.

This won't make your everyday file copies faster. It's a demonstration of where the cost actually lives.

A couple of notes for anyone who knows NTFS well enough to squint at this:

The header line the tool prints (sec=512 clu=4096 rec=1024 blocks=137 ext=1251 clusters) is just the geometry it detected for that run: sector size, cluster size, MFT record size, how many index blocks it built, and how many clusters it extended $MFT by.

Build DiskWriteCpp.sln in Visual Studio (Release | x64), or from the Developer Command Prompt:

This produces x64\Release\diskforge.exe (the DiskWriteCpp project builds a binary named diskforge.exe — the project folder just wasn't renamed on disk) and x64\Release\OriginalApproach.exe, the CreateFileW baseline from the comparison above.

It writes 5,000 files into G:\BULKDIR\. Swap G: for whatever drive letter you're willing to lose, and 5000 for however many files you want.

This is destructive and educational. It edits $MFT, $MFTMirr, and the volume bitmap by hand. A mistake in the run-list encoding or the index layout can leave the volume unmountable.

title: Specjudge, tells you which model you should use for each task
description: Local-first CLI that reads your Spec-Driven Development artifacts and recommends the best value-for-money AI model to implement them. Powered by Ollama — your specs never leave your machine. - Joaq...
fullText:
Stop guessing which AI model to use. Ask your specs.

SpecJudge reads your Spec-Driven Development artifacts and tells you which AI model actually
fits the job — before you spend a single token implementing it.

Here it is on a real spec — examples/task-manager, a small
CRUD web app, is included in this repo so you can run it yourself:

Abridged: the real run scores all 37 models in the catalog and lists every one of them. Prices and ratings above are generated from data/models.yaml, so they cannot go stale silently.

Mistral Small 3.2 24B (local) is right-sized for this project and costs nothing per token — it runs on your own hardware. Claude Fable 5, the priciest option this project does not need, bills $50.00/M output, $10.00/M input. If you would rather not self-host, the cheapest hosted model that still fits is DeepSeek V4 Flash at $0.28/M output, $0.14/M input — 179× cheaper on output than reaching for the frontier.

The demand profile was estimated once by a local judge and pinned, so this example is
reproducible without Ollama; everything else is generated from the live catalog.

Add --open for a visual matrix in your browser, filterable by model family and by open source.

You've finished defining a project with Spec-Driven Development. Now you have to pick a model to
implement it. Two expensive mistakes are waiting:

SpecJudge puts that decision at the one moment it's cheapest to make it: the specs exist, but
nothing has been spent yet. And it grounds the answer in your project, not a generic benchmark.

Requirements: Python 3.11+, uv, and
Ollama 0.5.0+ with at least one local model. The version matters:
asking the judge for cited evidence needs structured outputs, added in 0.5.0. On an older
Ollama the run stops with an error saying so — and how to proceed without citations.

That's it. On first run SpecJudge lists your local models, asks which one to use as the judge,
and remembers your choice.

📺 Prefer to watch? There's a
walkthrough on YouTube — in Spanish.

What's being worked on, what's next, and where help is wanted lives in a single
public roadmap issue — kept current there
rather than duplicated here, where it would rot.

The most useful contribution is keeping the model catalog accurate: models and prices change every
few weeks, and updating them takes zero Python. Several issues tagged
good first issue don't
require touching the code either.

The judge runs on your machine through Ollama. Your specs — your business logic, your design
decisions — never touch a third-party service, and deciding which model to buy costs you nothing
in API calls. The browser report is a self-contained HTML file that loads nothing from the network.

This isn't a nice-to-have; it's Principle I of the project constitution.

The judge estimates how demanding your project is across a few dimensions. Declarative rules in
rating-rules.yaml cross that demand against each model's declared capability. The best fit
wins — no black box, and every verdict comes with a reason you can read.

And the reason has to be more than well written. For each dimension the judge must cite the
fragment of your spec that supports its rating, and SpecJudge checks that fragment really exists
in the text it was given:

A judge that invents a citation has its whole assessment rejected, and one that cannot ground a
dimension answers unsupported rather than guessing — that dimension then leaves the calculation
instead of quietly counting as easy work.

This checks grounding, not relevance: a judge can cite something that exists but doesn't really
support the level, and no automatic check catches that. It is still a great deal more than a
paragraph that sounds convincing.

Every model gets a rating on a fixed scale:

The podium ranks models by how well they fit your project's complexity — neither under-capable
nor more powerful than needed.

Price does not decide the ranking. It's shown for every model so you can see what each option
costs, and it only breaks ties between models that fit equally well. A cheaper model never wins
over one that fits better — recommending something that can't do the job is the most expensive
mistake of all. Right-sizing is what keeps you from overpaying.

If no model in the catalog is capable enough, SpecJudge says so instead of recommending one
anyway. Same when your project is too thinly specified to judge — see Data states below.

Data states — SpecJudge is explicit about how much it can be trusted:

If your judge cannot manage cited evidence, set evidence.require_spans: false in
data/rating-rules.yaml to rate without it — you lose the grounding check in exchange.

Exit codes — degradation is distinguishable programmatically:

--json emits a payload with its own versioned schema, which you can fetch without
cloning anything:

That covers any language. From Python there is a small documented entry point:

Everything exported from specjudge.api is covered by semantic versioning; everything
else under specjudge.* is internal and changes without notice. The full surface, the
schema rules and what is deliberately not promised are in docs/api.md.

Models and prices change every few weeks. That's the whole reason this project needs you.

The most valuable contribution requires zero Python — SpecJudge keeps everything volatile in
human-readable data files, deliberately separate from the code. Adding a model is one YAML block:

Open data/models.yaml, add it, send the PR. Contract tests validate the schema automatically,
so a mistake can't slip through unnoticed.

Disagree with a rating? That's a contribution, not a complaint — the catalog is opinion made
inspectable. Open a PR with your reasoning.

See CONTRIBUTING.md for the full schemas and project governance.

Contributions that add mandatory paid dependencies to the core. A tool whose purpose is to save
you money must not require money to run. That's Principle III, and it isn't negotiable.

title: ICE asks North Carolina to hold illegal immigrant accused in toddler’s bathtub death
description: ICE has filed a detainer against an illegal immigrant accused of leaving his 14-month-old stepchild unattended in a bathtub. The child allegedly drowned, DHS said.
fullText:
EXCLUSIVE: Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) lodged a detainer against a criminal illegal alien who allegedly left a 14-month-old toddler to drown in a bathtub, according to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

The ICE detainer asks North Carolina officials not to release Angel Israel Deras-Rivas, a Salvadoran national who was arrested Sunday in Garner.

DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin criticized the Biden administration's immigration policies, arguing they contributed to the circumstances surrounding the case.

"This criminal illegal alien has been charged with murder and felony child abuse after letting a 14-month-old drown in a bathtub," Mullin said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

Exclusive: Dhs Seeks Custody Of Illegal Immigrant Charged With Murder After Trump Deportation, Biden Release

Deras-Rivas, 19, was caring for his stepchild when he allegedly left the toddler unattended in a bathtub filled with water, resulting in the child's death, according to an arrest warrant cited by The Raleigh News & Observer. The incident happened just months after Deras-Rivas married the child's mother in April, the outlet reported.

Immigration officials said Deras-Rivas, identified by DHS as a criminal illegal alien, unlawfully entered the United States through Texas in October 2023 and was released into the country by the Biden administration.

Ice Urges North Carolina To Keep Illegal Immigrant Charged In Triple-fatal Hit-and-run Behind Bars

"That child would still be alive today if it weren't for the reckless open-border policies of the Biden administration that released this criminal into our country in the first place. ICE is calling on officials in North Carolina to commit to not releasing this killer from jail, and to turn him over to ICE custody so we can get him out of our country."

Immigration officials said ICE filed the detainer with the Wake County Sheriff's Department on the same day Deras-Rivas was arrested.

An ICE detainer typically requests that local law enforcement notify the agency before an individual's release and hold the person for up to 48 additional hours beyond a scheduled release date, allowing ICE agents time to take the individual into federal custody for potential removal proceedings.

Fox News Digital reached out to the Garner Police Department

title: Who will leave Chelsea? How Blues could cut 41-man squad
description: With 25 days until the transfer window closes, Chelsea will be working hard to cut their 41-man senior squad. But who could be heading out?
fullText:
Chelsea are in the familiar position of having a large number of players on their books, with 41 senior players and only 25 days remaining in the transfer window to resolve the situation.

With no European football this campaign, new boss Xabi Alonso is keen to significantly reduce his squad - with a number of players either available for sale or on loan.

While the Blues can effectively register as many players as they want, despite the Premier League's 25-man squad rule - with under-21 and homegrown regulations covering the vast majority of players on their books - the Spaniard knows having players not involved cannot be good for squad harmony.

But, even to get the squad down to a more manageable 25 senior players, Chelsea will need to offload 16 players by the start of September.

The Blues have had players stranded in a 'bomb squad' in the past, like Raheem Sterling and Axel Disasi last season. That practice has since been outlawed by Fifa, increasing the importance of drastically reducing the squad.

Had Chelsea qualified for Europe they would have been at risk of being unable to register certain players, as was the case during their 2024-25 Conference League-winning campaign.

They are also bound by a Uefa settlement agreement for three more seasons, but European football's governing body has acknowledged they have made efforts to improve their finances.

The Blues are accustomed to this level of player trading and are boosted by the fact they have largely built Alonso's squad through the signings of Morgan Rogers, Marco Palestra, Danny Welbeck, Jordan Henderson and Maxence Lacroix, with full-back Pep Chavarria close to joining from Rayo Vallecano.

The size of the squad is an issue that needs addressing though. On Wednesday, they had 21 substitutes for their 1-0 defeat by Juventus in Hong Kong. Just five were academy players.

Chelsea were keen to carry a large squad into the final few days of their Asian tour. They face AC Milan in Indonesia on Saturday before taking on Malaysian champions Johor Darul Ta'zim on Sunday and will likely field two different XIs.

But, it remains a remarkable number given both Cole Palmer and Levi Colwill were absent from the midweek match because of knocks sustained in the previous friendly, and striker Emmanuel Emegha is continuing his rehabilitation from a hamstring injury at the training ground.

There are also five players not even training with the first team: Benoit Badiashile, Axel Disasi, Marc Guiu, David Datro Fofana and Caleb Wiley. They are all available either for permanent or loan moves.

Seven players remain on holiday until next week having featured in the latter stages of the World Cup: Enzo Fernandez, Reece James, Rogers, Henderson, Lacroix, Valentin Barco and Malo Gusto.

Defender Trevoh Chalobah is close to joining Como for £31m, including add-ons, while goalkeeper Filip Jorgensen is joining sister club Strasbourg on loan.

Chelsea nearing £16.3m deal for Rayo defender Chavarria

Mudryk returns after 20 months out in Chelsea defeat

Chelsea are out of European football next season after finishing 10th in a campaign where Enzo Maresca left the club and Liam Rosenior was dismissed.

Alonso has some difficult decisions ahead.

His goalkeeping options appear set, with Robert Sanchez joined by exciting Belgian prospect Mike Penders, 21, following his impressive loan spell at French club Strasbourg, with with Teddy Sharman-Lowe likely to serve as the third-choice understudy.

At full-back, club captain Reece James, also capable of playing in midfield, is joined on the right by Gusto and Palestra.

Chelsea have put a £75m price tag on Gusto after Manchester City emerged as potential suitors.

On the left, Chelsea have Jorrel Hato and are close to completing the £16.3m signing of Chavarria.

At centre-back, Chelsea have nine players and Alonso has said the group needs reducing to "four or five".

Disasi and Badiashile are available for sale, while Mamadou Sarr is expected to depart on loan. That would leave new signing Lacroix competing with Levi Colwill, Josh Acheampong, Wesley Fofana and Tosin Adarabioyo.

It remains unclear what will happen with Argentina Under-20 international Aaron Anselmino, although another loan move appears likely having spent last term with Borussia Dortmund and Strasbourg.

In midfield Chelsea have put a £120m price tag on Fernandez, who is exploring his options, although the club would also be happy to keep him.

He is joined by fellow key central midfielder Moises Caicedo, fit-again Romeo Lavia, new signing Barco, who can play a number of positions in that area, Henderson and Dario Essugo.

Essugo, 21, was previously told he would be staying but is open to a loan move because of his need for regular football after an injury-hit campaign.

In attack, the shock return of Mykhailo Mudryk is another situation Chelsea must manage.

The club insist all options remain open and are assessing his fitness following his return after 20 months out, because of a suspension relating to a positive test for the banned substance meldonium.

Jamie Gittens is another option on the left wing, while Pedro Neto and new arrival Geovany Quenda are primarily right-sided players. Cole Palmer and Rogers are the two number 10s.

Chelsea would also like to have three strikers going into next season. Alongside Joao Pedro and summer signing Welbeck, one further forward is likely to remain in the squad.

That looks likely to be Emegha, although there remains uncertainty given Chelsea also have Nicolas Jackson and Liam Delap on their books.

There is some overlap but, from information gathered by BBC Sport to date, this is the best projection of what Chelsea's squad could look like.

Projected Chelsea squad: Sanchez, Penders, Sharman-Lowe, James, Palestra, Tosin, Fofana, Lacroix, Acheampong, Colwill, Hato, Chavarria, Caicedo, Fernandez, Barco, Lavia, Henderson, Quenda, Neto, Palmer, Estevao, Rogers, Gittens, Emegha, Joao Pedro, Welbeck.

Available for loan: Guiu, Wiley, Kellyman, Mheuka, Walsh, Kavuma-McQueen, Kendry Paez.

Available for sale/uncertain futures, with desired fees for some players in brackets: Badiashile (£30m), Disasi (£25m), Guiu (£25m), Datro Fofana, Delap, Jackson (£65m), Slonina, Gusto (£75m), Fernandez (£120m), Emegha, Neto, Essugo.

Alonso heals Real Madrid scars to lead Chelsea's senior revolution

Chelsea have been stockpiling players for more than a decade, dating back to former owner Roman Abramovich's reign.

Under Abramovich, they had as many as 42 players out on loan before Fifa introduced limits designed to curb the practice.

However, since Todd Boehly and Clearlake Capital took charge in 2022 Chelsea have acquired Strasbourg, adding to the growing number of multi-club ownership models across Europe.

They also embarked on a strategy of signing younger players on lower wages, who can be moved in and out as required.

Among those signings was midfielder Andrey Santos, who arrived for £12m after a season in Brazil's second division before being sold to Manchester United for £50m.

Chelsea have spent £1.8bn on acquiring talent since BlueCo took over the club four years ago, comfortably more than any other club in Europe.

However, they have also raised nearly £1bn through player sales, including a Premier League record £300m, again the highest figure in Europe during that period.

Chelsea are expected to make a similar number of sales this summer, with Chalobah's move to Como taking their total beyond £150m and Alejandro Garnacho's loan move to Aston Villa including an obligation to buy set to be worth about £40m next summer.

They have the lowest revenues among the traditional 'big six' clubs.

That is largely because of the size of Stamford Bridge, commercial underperformance, a kit deal with Adidas that has not kept pace with rivals, the absence of a front-of-shirt sponsor and missing out on Champions League football in three of the past four seasons.

It is player trading that makes up much of that shortfall, in much the same way as it does for Brighton, Brentford and Bournemouth, albeit with loftier ambitions of winning trophies and qualifying for the Champions League.

title: Crowded Russian beach descends into chaos after alleged Ukrainian drone incident kills 7, including 4 children
description: A projectile struck a crowded Russian Black Sea beach Monday, killing seven people, including four children, and injuring 58. Russia blamed a Ukrainian drone attack as video captured the deadly impact...
fullText:
Vacationers were sent scrambling for safety Monday after a projectile struck a crowded beach in a Russian Black Sea resort town, killing seven people, including four children, and injuring dozens more, officials said.

Video footage captured the incident in the village of Arkhipo-Osipovka near Gelendzhik, where the beach was packed with visitors at the time of the strike.

The Russian Mission in Geneva said in a post on X that the "bloody attack" was carried out by a drone launched by Ukraine, accusing Kyiv of targeting civilians.

Ukraine Launches What Appears To Be One Of Its Largest Drone Attacks Against Russia: Report

"The attack targeted civilian infrastructure. Emergency and special services are working at the crash site," regional Gov. Veniamin Kondratyev said in a post on Telegram.

"What happened today is a targeted attack by the Kyiv regime against civilians who have no connection to the military infrastructure. This cynical and inhumane terrorist attack against children cannot be justified."

Ukraine Unleashes More Than 400 Drones Near Moscow In One Of War's Biggest Attacks

Andriy Kovalenko, an officer with Ukraine's Defense Forces, disputed Russia's account, saying the deaths were directly caused by Russian air defenses that intercepted a drone, sending debris onto the beach.

"Russian air defense shot down a drone over people lying on the beach," Kovalenko said on Telegram.

In the video, sounds resembling gunfire were heard just seconds before a drone struck the beach, causing a fireball explosion that sent bystanders screaming. As the gunfire was heard, the drone appeared to veer sharply before diving toward the beach.

Preliminary Russian reports also found that several of the deaths were caused by "falling drone debris," Kondratyev said.

Zelenskyy Says Putin 'Lost The Initiative' As Ukraine's Tech Industry Reshapes The War

In another Telegram post, Kovalenko indicated that Ukraine uses its weapons against Russian military-industrial infrastructure to affect Moscow's ability to finance the war.

He further accused Russian President Vladimir Putin of creating an "illusion" that Russia would remain safe from the war by downplaying daily explosions as falling debris, limiting air raid warnings, and positioning air defenses near populated areas such as the Black Sea resort.

"Putin deliberately killed these people. Because if he had not started the war and struck Ukraine, they would be alive," Kovalenko said.

"It was Putin, his air defense, who killed these Russians. His decisions in response to their decisions launched a chain of death for Russians."

title: Former US Marine Robert Gilman may be near death in Russian prison
description: Allegedly tortured and injected with mind-altering drugs, he is believe to have been in a stupor since June and may be close to death, his family says.
fullText:
Note: the video above is from an interview in February, 2026.

WASHINGTON (Reuters) – A former U.S. Marine jailed in Russia since 2022 and allegedly tortured and injected with mind-altering drugs, slipped into a stupor in June and may be close to death, according to two hostage advocacy groups and his sister.

The White House and the State Department have urged Moscow to release Robert Gilman, 32, so he can receive urgent medical treatment in the U.S., said Eric Lebson, chief strategy officer of Global Reach, an advocacy group representing his family. Gilman is being fed through a tube, he said.

A source familiar with the matter told Reuters they had learned through State Department contacts that Secretary of State Marco Rubio raised the case with Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov during a meeting in Manila on July 23.

The source, speaking on condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the matter, said they did not know Lavrov's response.

Gilman is one of at least 10 Americans known to be imprisoned in Russia. His death would complicate Washington's ties with Moscow, already strained by the Iran and Ukraine wars and other issues.

"I am more afraid for my brother than I have been since this horrible nightmare started," Lexie Hudson, Gilman's sister, said in a statement. "I'm worried that I may never see him again if the Russians don't release him. I'm worried that he could die."

A senior Trump administration official, who was also granted anonymity, said the administration "is closely tracking Mr. Gilman's case and has made repeated, concerted outreach to the Russians calling for his return to the United States."

"We are deeply concerned about Robert Gilman's health and continued detention," the State Department said in a statement.

The Russian embassy did not respond to requests for comment.

The Russian hospital has barred Gilman's mother from visiting him even though she has a judicial order that she be permitted to see her son, Lebson said.

U.S. consular officials were occasionally allowed to visit Gilman in prison, but neither they nor his Russian lawyer have been permitted into the hospital, he added.

Gilman was being held in a prison in Voronezh, about 340 miles (547 kilometers) south of Moscow. He was moved in late June from the prison hospital to the psychiatric ward of a civilian emergency hospital in a catatonic-like state assessed as a "dissociative stupor," said Lebson.

The World Health Organization's ICD-10, an internationally used diagnostic classification system, describes a dissociative stupor as "a profound diminution or absence of voluntary movement and normal responsiveness to external stimuli."

Gilman has been unable to communicate, must receive food and fluids through a tube and his eyes remain shut, Lebson said. The condition has prevented him from attending court hearings.

"It doesn't seem like he's getting the care he needs, and we are very concerned for his life and safety," said Elizabeth Richards, director of hostage advocacy and research at the Foley Foundation, a group that has tracked the case.

A Russian newspaper on July 9 reported Gilman had been moved to a hospital in Voronezh, and quoted his lawyer as saying it was too early for a diagnosis.

Gilman, who served in the U.S. Marines from August 2019 until August 2020, was traveling by train when he was arrested on January 17, 2022, in Voronezh, Lebson said.

He was detained for allegedly kicking a police officer while drunk, according to Russian state media.

However, his father, Vladimir Gilman, who immigrated to Massachusetts from Russia, wrote in an October 11, 2024, Boston Globe op-ed that the charges were false.

His son, he said, had fallen ill when the incident occurred and accidentally kicked the officer. The officer was uninjured, dropped the charges, and did not present evidence in Robert Gilman's trial, he wrote.

Robert Gilman was sentenced to 4-1/2 years in jail.

Vladimir Gilman wrote that the family had asked the State Department in March 2023 to designate his son as wrongfully detained, a designation that would make winning his release a top U.S. government priority.

Russian state media reported that Robert Gilman's sentence was extended in 2024 to 10 years for allegedly assaulting prison staff.

Lebson and Richards denied that allegation, saying that Robert Gilman was held in extremely harsh conditions, tortured and injected with mind-altering drugs by guards, treatment that led to his transfer to the civilian hospital.

"We are seriously worried that we could see another situation like Otto Warmbier," Lebson said.

He was referring to a U.S. college student who was comatose when he was freed in June 2017 by North Korea after 17 months in prison. Warmbier died the same month in a U.S. hospital from severe brain damage of an unknown cause without regaining consciousness.

title: Florida man accused of cutting off diver's air supply in fight over coveted lobster diving spot
description: A dispute over a lobster diving spot during Florida's lobster mini season allegedly turned deadly when a man shut off a diver's surface supplied air.
fullText:
A battle over a lobster diving spot off the Florida coast allegedly escalated into an underwater nightmare after a man was accused of shutting off another diver's air supply, a confrontation that landed him behind bars on an attempted murder charge.

Michael Joseph Simpson, 51, surrendered Tuesday to the Turner Guilford Knight Correctional Center in Miami-Dade County, where he was booked Tuesday evening on an attempted murder charge, according to Miami-Dade jail records. His bond was set at $10,000.

According to Local 10 News, the incident occurred shortly after 7 a.m. on July 29 about a half-mile east of Fisher Island during Florida's annual lobster mini season.

Citing the arrest affidavit, Law&Crime reported that Simpson allegedly approached another boat at a high rate of speed and circled the vessel several times before anchoring about 10 feet away.

Florida Man Arrested For Dui After Troopers Allegedly Find 34 Open Alcohol Containers In Vehicle

Investigators say the confrontation began after Simpson claimed the group was diving in "his spot" and warned that a larger boat was on its way before it arrived and anchored nearby.

Authorities allege Simpson then threatened to turn off the surface-supplied air system providing oxygen to an 18-year-old diver searching for lobsters. Investigators say Simpson jumped into the water and intentionally shut off the unit.

As the confrontation unfolded, witnesses yelled, "We have a diver down there you a--hole!" according to the arrest affidavit cited by Law&Crime.

The diver's boat owner jumped into the water and pulled him to the surface. The diver was gasping for air and appeared disoriented but was not injured, Local 10 reported.

Florida Man Gives An Incredible Interview About How He Fought Off An Alligator With A Fishing Pole

Investigators allege Simpson left before deputies arrived. After authorities identified him as the suspect, Simpson voluntarily surrendered Tuesday, according to Local 10.

Simpson's attorney, Howard Srebnick, strongly denied the allegations in a statement to Fox News Digital, arguing investigators ignored evidence and witnesses he says support his client's account.

Srebnick said Simpson was diving from his own boat with friends and his two young children and "never disabled anyone's diving equipment."

Srebnick said video shows one of the accusers becoming entangled in the Brownie's Third Lung air system while Simpson "was nowhere near it."

American Tourist Attacked By Shark In Vacation Hot Spot

He also disputed investigators' allegation that Simpson fled, saying his client instead idled his boat away from the immediate area to avoid escalating the confrontation before cooperating with responding Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission officers and providing a statement.

Srebnick said numerous eyewitnesses aboard two separate boats corroborated Simpson's version of events and criticized the Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office for arresting his client before interviewing what he described as exculpatory witnesses.

"We are optimistic that the State Attorney's Office, after reviewing the video and interviewing all the eyewitnesses, will dismiss the charges, clear his name, and restore the reputation he has spent a lifetime building," Srebnick said.

Fox News Digital has reached out to the Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office for additional comment.

title: Man in court after cocaine worth £2m seized on A14

fullText:
A man charged with drug offences after police seized cocaine worth more than £2m has appeared in court.

Arminas Sotikovas, 35, of Riverside Road in Ipswich, has been charged with possession of a Class A drug with intent to supply.

Suffolk Police said officers stopped a white van travelling on the eastbound carriageway of the A14, near Stowmarket, on Tuesday when they found the large quantity of cocaine.

Sotikovas appeared at Ipswich Magistrates' Court where he was remanded into custody ahead of his next hearing at Ipswich Crown Court on 3 September.
