title: Iowa Democratic Senate nominee slams Democrats on Agriculture panel over farm bill failure
description: Iowa state Rep. Josh Turek, the Democratic nominee for Iowa’s Senate race, criticized Democratic lawmakers on a congressional panel who voted against the annual farm bill Thursday. All of the Democrat...
fullText:
Iowa state Rep. Josh Turek, the Democratic nominee for Iowa's Senate race, criticized Democratic lawmakers on a congressional panel who voted against the annual farm bill Thursday.

All of the Democrats on the Senate Agriculture Committee voted to block the funding package from advancing to the Senate floor over a dispute surrounding the bill's food aid provisions.

Turek, who won his party's nomination for U.S. Senate in the state's Democratic primary in June, represents a state House district that has voted for President Trump in the past three presidential elections.

Turek has championed his bipartisan voting record in the state House and promised to "tackle Washington's rampant corruption" if elected this fall.

"Iowa farmers have been waiting three years for an overdue Farm Bill, and today Democrats in the Senate failed them by letting perfect be the enemy of the good," Turek said in a statement shared on social media.

"To be clear: I would have voted in support of this Farm Bill," he continued. "This is just another example of a fundamentally broken Washington, and as Iowa's next U.S. Senator, I'll work with anyone to pass a damn Farm Bill — and I'll make it so Congress can't recess without passing one. Our farmers deserve no less."

Turek is up against Iowa Rep. Ashley Hinson (R) in the November midterm election.

The GOP lawmaker responded to her Democratic opponent's statement about the farm bill in a social media post, slamming Turek over his past support for California's new pesticide and animal confinement requirements.

"Josh's talk is cheap on this after Iowa farmers were outraged over his support for Prop 12 and against my Save our Bacon Act included in the Farm Bill," Hinson wrote in the post. "Unfortunately for Josh, Iowans know he's got about $30 million reasons to keep siding with Chuck Schumer against Iowa farmers," she said, referencing the Senate Democratic leader from New York.

Democrats on the Senate Agriculture Committee opposed the funding package Thursday after the panel's chair, Sen. John Boozman (R-Ark.), refused to meet their demands on food aid legislation.

Ranking member Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) and other Democrats on the panel have pushed the chair to delay a provision requiring states to share the cost of providing Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits by two years.

Democrats have said the current proposal unfairly burdens states with mid-level SNAP error rates while rewarding those with high error rates.

Boozman offered a one-year delay, but the ranking member said this was not enough time to allow states to reduce SNAP error rates.

Sen. Michael Bennet (Colo.), one of the Democrats who opposed the bill's advancement over its SNAP provisions, said in a Thursday statement that he was "disappointed" that a bipartisan solution had not been reached.

"At a time when families are already struggling to afford groceries, Republicans are working to make SNAP even more inaccessible, all while placing the financial burden on states and the backs of hardworking families," Bennet wrote in a social media post. "For Colorado, this bill would be a devastating blow to our already strained budget."

Klobuchar said after the vote Thursday that she was "committed" to working with Boozman to pass this legislation. The Republican chair announced he would reconvene the committee after Senate recess concludes in September to reconsider the bill.

"I'm deeply disappointed Democrats on the Ag Committee voted against advancing a farm bill," Boozman said in a social media statement. "We have a responsibility to stand with America's farmers, ranchers and rural communities. Everyone recognizes the serious challenges they continue to face, and blocking the farm bill only adds to the uncertainty and hardship."

In addition to unified votes from Democrats against the bill, absences from two of the panel's GOP members blocked the bill's advancement out of committee.

Sens. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) and Tommy Tuberville (R-Ala.) voted by proxy and were therefore not included in the final vote tally of 10-11. The bill needed support from a majority of the panel to advance to the floor for a final vote on its passage.

The Hill has reached out to the offices of both GOP lawmakers for a comment about their absence from the vote. McConnell has not cast a vote in Congress since he sustained a fall in June. The Kentucky senator said he was released from a rehabilitation facility Thursday and is recovering at home during recess.

title: Oil settles up $3 as Iran reviews bill to ban US, Israeli vessels from Hormuz
description: Oil prices settled up by more than $3 a barrel on Thursday on news an Iranian parliament committee is reviewing a bill that would ban U.S. and Israeli
fullText:
HOUSTON, Aug 6 (Reuters) - Oil prices settled up by more than $3 a barrel on Thursday on news an Iranian parliament committee is reviewing a bill that would ban U.S. and Israeli vessels from the ‌Strait of Hormuz and fine violators up to a fifth of the value of their cargo.

Brent crude futures ‌settled up $3.04, or 3.83%, to $82.49 a barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures settled up $2.07, or 2.75%, to $77.29.

What impact are Houthi attacks having on oil supplies?

How are geopolitical tensions affecting Gulf oil exports?

What drove oil prices up over $3 per barrel?

How could Iran's Strait of Hormuz bill affect shipping?

An Iranian lawmaker said a parliament committee is reviewing a ​preliminary bill to ban U.S., Israeli and other vessels deemed hostile from the Strait of Hormuz, and fine violators of the proposed restrictions up to 20% of cargo value, according to Fars news agency.

"Crude traders remain focused on the U.S./Iran agreements, and the longer the delays, the more prices will fade back to the upside," said Dennis Kissler, senior vice president of trading at BOK Financial.

Before the ‌Iran conflict began in late February, about one-fifth ⁠of global daily oil and liquefied natural gas supplies flowed through the Strait of Hormuz.

Meanwhile, Yemen's Houthis said they carried out missile and drone attacks on "Saudi deployments" in Marib and Hadramout in Yemen ⁠on Thursday, and that they killed or wounded hundreds of Saudi-aligned fighters, and destroyed military camps, weapons depots and vehicles.

"The market is going up and down as tensions rise and fall and of course these attacks are a significant development because it is more activity in ​the other ​theatre, away from the Persian Gulf, and is a reminder that ​the Red Sea passageway could still be in jeopardy," ‌said John Kilduff, partner at Again Capital.

Gulf countries' crude oil and condensate exports were largely steady in July and remained about 40% below pre-war levels, shipping data showed.

Iran has warned Gulf states that any new U.S. attack on its territory would trigger attacks on critical energy infrastructure across the region, according to five sources, as Tehran seeks to raise the cost of military action by threatening Washington's closest regional allies.

The Iran-aligned Houthis said on Wednesday they had launched a missile attack on a ‌Saudi oil tanker off the coast of the kingdom's Red Sea port ​city of Yanbu and another missile attack on a Saudi oil tanker in ​the nearby Gulf of Aden. There was no confirmation ​from Saudi Arabia on either incident.

"Houthi attacks so far have not significantly disrupted oil and gas supply ‌but this might change if attacks escalate further," said ​Roberto Cominotto, equity research analyst ​at Julius Baer.

title: Democratic strategist James Carville says he could become a Republican under one major condition
description: Veteran Democratic strategist James Carville revealed the only hypothetical scenario in which he'd join the Republican Party as Hasan Piker and democratic socialists gain ground.
fullText:
Veteran Democratic strategist James Carville told Fox News Digital Thursday there is only one unlikely scenario in which he would actually join the Republican Party.

Posed with a hypothetical where Republicans had the policies of former President Bill Clinton from the 1990s and the Democratic Party fully embraced socialism, Carville said, "That's a fantasy, OK, but, yeah, hypothetically, if I — hypothetically I could fly to the moon — it's about the same chance that that happens.

"Well, if the Democrats went crazy and the Republicans went sane, then I probably would be a Republican," he added. "But I don't see any evidence that there's any possibility that the latter could happen.

"I think it's more likely than not that the Democrats embrace sanity," Carville continued, saying the party's direction will be determined by Democratic primary voters.

Hasan Piker's Defense Of Hamas Having 'Right To Resist Militarily' Draws Condemnation From Human Rights Groups

In recent months, there has been a rising faction of far-left Democratic candidates in multiple states to the point Carville has suggested there be a schism to keep them out of power.

Hasan Piker, a self-described socialist streamer who campaigned with Democratic Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, has emerged as a leading voice on the left as democratic socialists gain ground in elections across the country.

Piker is known for far-left rhetoric, including previously saying "America deserved 9/11." After widespread criticism, Piker said in an interview he "obviously" did not mean America deserved the attacks and defended the viral quote as a critique of U.S. foreign policy.

"I am not going to be in the same party with Hasan Piker," Carville said recently on Fox News' "The Sunday Briefing." "If he becomes a force in a Democratic Party, I'm out of here. I have no intention of ever being in the same political party with that guy."

Speaking to Fox News Digital on Thursday, Carville addressed what would happen if the socialist faction took over the Democratic Party.

"That probably would result in some kind of schism in the party," he reiterated. "I'm going to let Democratic voters determine the direction that party goes in, and if it goes in the direction — which I'm pretty confident it won't — but if it goes in that direction, then I'm going to be 82, OK, fine, go ahead, but not with me.

"Until Democratic voters choose the direction of the party, I'll try to do all I can to help them make the right choice, in my opinion."

John Fetterman Makes It 'Very Clear' That He's 'Not Going To Be A Republican' Despite Dem Backlash

Carville's threat to leave the Democratic Party has been mocked by its progressive wing.

"Now James Carville is talking about leaving the party," Piker said during a recent video appearance with El-Sayed. "We got [Pennsylvania Sen.] John Fetterman, James Carville fantasizing about leaving the party. I'm like, 'You're sweetening the deal.' That was really interesting."

Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., has also stood by Piker after Carville's warning.

"Well, that's not much of a choice," Sanders said of choosing between Piker and Carville. "If Mr. Carville doesn't want to be in my party, the party that I belong to, that Piker, that El-Sayed belongs to, he can start his own party."

title: Uganda midfielder Owori murdered in street gang attack
description: The 27-year-old was killed by suspected robbers after resisting an attempt to rob him, police say.
fullText:
Ugandans are mourning the death at 27 of one of the country's best-known footballers after he was beaten by suspected robbers near his home in the capital, Kampala.

Police said David Owori was fatally assaulted after resisting an attempt to steal his mobile phone and other belongings, prompting an outpouring of grief and renewed public anger over violent crime in Uganda.

Owori captained Sports Club (SC) Villa, the Uganda Premier League record champions, where he played both as a right-back and midfielder. He also represented the country's national team - the Cranes.

"We have lost more than a player - we have lost a leader, brother and friend," SC Villa said in a statement.

Witnesses said a group of attackers hit the footballer with paving stones on Tuesday night before robbing Owori of his belongings and fleeing, leaving him unconscious.

SC Villa spokesperson Asan Kasingye told journalists that Owori was targeted just outside his home in Makindye, a Kampala suburb.

"The player was ambushed by thugs as he approached his home, leaving him with life-threatening injuries before he was rushed to the medical facility," Kasingye said.

Owori was rushed to a nearby medical clinic and then transferred to a private facility in the city, but he died of his injuries on Wednesday.

Local police spokesperson Rachael Kawala said detectives were pursuing leads to identify those responsible.

"The scene of the incident has been documented and processed to ensure that all relevant evidence is collected and preserved," Kawala added.

Owori's murder has sent shockwaves across Uganda, with the football community, including fans and teammates, and politicians demanding justice.

Tributes are continuing to pour in for the defender, who was popularly known as Colgate.

The Federation of Uganda Football Associations (Fufa) described Owori as "a true leader on and off the pitch".

"David was not just a footballer. He was both a leader and an inspiration to a generation," it said in a statement.

The national side, the Cranes, said the team had lost a football star who "carried the hopes" of Uganda.

Parliament on Wednesday observed a minute's silence in honour of Owori and called for a quick investigation.

The versatile player, renowned for his tactical discipline and ability to feature across midfield, returned to SC Villa in 2023 - after two years in Europe - for a second spell. At the time of his death, he was among the longest-serving members of the current squad.

He helped lead the high-profile team to their first league title in 20 years securing a record 17th top-flight crown in 2024.

His influence on and off the pitch earned him a contract extension until January 2027 with the team.

Owori also featured in the national team during the 2021 Africa Cup of Nations qualifying campaign and was regarded as a strong contender for future call-ups to the Cranes.

His death has triggered anger on social media, with many Ugandans questioning the level of violent crime in Kampala and calling for tougher action against criminals.

The killing comes just weeks after the death of another Ugandan sports star - rugby international Sydney Gongodyo - who was also fatally attacked by a mob in Kampala
